chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 381 to 390, Othalanthaiyar's paalai decade of words spoken on the waste road during an elopement (உடன்போக்கின் கண் இடைச் சுரத்து உரைத்த பத்து): onlookers pity and admire the couple, the hamlet's mothers grieve, the youth delights in the girl's play, the girl sends word home to her companions and her mother, and travellers and brahmins answer the searching mother or foster mother.

381.reading: Onlookers on the road see a pair who ate green nelli fruit together and sit in the striped shade of a red-stemmed maraam, and ask who these pitiable ones are, then answer: lovers whose way is to stay joined, like the long-winged, short-legged magandril.
381.nuance: அளியர் is pity and tenderness at once: the onlookers' question begins as concern for two young people in the waste and ends as admiration, since the magandril pair was held never to part. Eating the sour nelli together is a wasteland meal shared, not a hardship borne alone.

thinai_evidence.note: lovers gone off together through the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: kandor
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (உடன்போக்கின் கண் இடைச் சுரத்து உரைத்த பத்து) places every poem on the road during the elopement; onlookers on the road speak among themselves about the couple

382.reading: She whose eyes start at every bird-call crosses the hard waste with a youth of white spear and fine war-anklets; in the noisy small hamlet where they rested at nightfall, the housewives who have borne jewelled daughters of their own feel great pain.
382.nuance: The pain is not the girl's but that of strangers: the hamlet's mothers see their own daughters in her and feel ahead of time the loss her mother has suffered. Her fear of birds marks how new she is to the road.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl crosses the waste with the youth

thurai_akam.speaker: kandor
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (உடன்போக்கின் கண் இடைச் சுரத்து உரைத்த பத்து) places every poem on the road during the elopement; the speaker reports how the hamlet where the couple rested took their passing

383.reading: In the wasteland where bees hum after honey, the warrior who stood holding a low branch of the tall maraam to pluck its white curling clusters was glad at heart, watching the girl of soft lovely hair choose flowers for her rush doll and for herself.
383.nuance: The girl is still a child: she adorns her பஞ்சாய்ப் பாவை, a doll of rush, before herself, and the youth's joy is in that play. The poem shows the eloping man as one who bends the branch for her rather than as a captor.

thinai_evidence.note: the maraam of the waste and the road

thurai_akam.speaker: kandor
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (உடன்போக்கின் கண் இடைச் சுரத்து உரைத்த பத்து) places every poem on the road during the elopement; an onlooker describes the youth watching the girl at play

384.reading: The girl asks slow-walking brahmins bound for a far land to carry one word to her bangled companions in her town: she has crossed the hard road so that the beauty her mother lovingly raised may flourish.
384.nuance: She frames the elopement as the fulfilment of her mother's care rather than its betrayal: the beauty the mother tended (ஆய் நயந்து எடுத்த) will now come to its bloom. The message goes to the companions, not to the mother.

thinai_evidence.note: she has crossed the hard road

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (உடன்போக்கின் கண் இடைச் சுரத்து உரைத்த பத்து) places every poem on the road during the elopement; the girl speaks to travelling brahmins (அந்தணிர்) going toward her town

385.reading: The girl asks travellers on the road to tell her mother, who without justice praised her fine shoulders and kept her undone at home, that she has mounted the tall chariot with the fierce youth, left behind the hill of the killing tiger, and crossed many hard wastes.
385.nuance: அறனில் யாய் turns the charge of wrong back on the mother: the guard that kept a grown girl at home is what the daughter calls unjust. The chariot and the tiger's hill leave no doubt that she went freely and far.

thinai_evidence.note: she has crossed the wastes with the youth

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (உடன்போக்கின் கண் இடைச் சுரத்து உரைத்த பத்து) places every poem on the road during the elopement; the girl speaks to wayfarers (ஆறுசெல் மாக்கள்) and sends word to her mother

386.reading: Through the waste where tigers range among distressed elephants, your first-born daughter has gone joined with the lover she desired: so the speaker tells the mother, who wanders bewildered in her tall-walled house like a lost ant.
386.nuance: On this reading உறவி (ant) is a vocative: the mother, searching every corner of the walled house, is pictured as an ant lost inside it, and the walls that guarded the girl now only trap the mother. கடுஞ்சூல் மகள், the child of the first pregnancy, sharpens her loss.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter has gone through the waste with her lover

thurai_akam.speaker: kandor
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (உடன்போக்கின் கண் இடைச் சுரத்து உரைத்த பத்து) places every poem on the road during the elopement; someone who has seen the couple tells the mother; நின் கடுஞ்சூல் மகள் names her as the one who bore the girl

387.reading: Brahmins whose tongues have practised the rare scripture devoted to right answer the simple bangled woman who says she will worship them as she asks: we saw her in the waste, her sweet companion fondly caressing her, as she crossed the mountain of piled rocks.
387.nuance: The searcher's worship of the brahmins as men of அறம் gives their answer weight: what they report is not danger but tenderness (இன் துணை இனிது பாராட்ட), so their eyewitness word is itself a quiet verdict on the match.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl has crossed the waste and the hills

thurai_akam.speaker: pira
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (உடன்போக்கின் கண் இடைச் சுரத்து உரைத்த பத்து) places every poem on the road during the elopement; the speakers are the brahmins (அந்தணிர்); the searching woman is the foster mother by the usual pattern of this situation, though the poem does not name her

388.reading: Travellers tell the searching woman to rest in the striped shade of the black-stemmed yaa until the fiery sun's heat abates; past the little hill she will see the waste toward which the youth of conquering spear went with the gold-skinned girl of close bangles.
388.nuance: The advice is practical and kind: the wayfarers do not dissuade her but tell her when and where to go, so the pursuit is treated as a journey to be managed, not a grief to be argued away.

thinai_evidence.note: the blazing sun of the wasteland

thurai_akam.speaker: pira
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (உடன்போக்கின் கண் இடைச் சுரத்து உரைத்த பத்து) places every poem on the road during the elopement; travellers on the road speak to the woman following the couple

389.reading: The searching woman, told that her doll-like girl of fine bangles went slowly with the youth of dark beard and strong war-anklets, asks the men whether her feet with their lovely anklets kept pace with his.
389.nuance: Told that the youth walked slowly (பைய), she asks not whether the girl suffered but whether the two were in step, so the worry turns to whether the match itself fits. The anklets still on her feet mark a girl not yet wed by rite.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl has gone with the youth

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (உடன்போக்கின் கண் இடைச் சுரத்து உரைத்த பத்து) places every poem on the road during the elopement; the woman who follows the couple speaks to men who have seen them (ஐய); the tradition makes her the foster mother

390.reading: Onlookers tell the woman who goes round and round, folding her hands in worship to every good person and asking, that they surely saw the girl in the waste with the youth of strong shoulders and mighty bow.
390.nuance: மன்ற (surely) answers the searcher's repeated asking: the onlookers give certainty, not comfort, and the youth is described by his strength, as one who can guard her.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl is with the youth in the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: kandor
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (உடன்போக்கின் கண் இடைச் சுரத்து உரைத்த பத்து) places every poem on the road during the elopement; onlookers answer the searching woman; the tradition makes her the foster mother

links.note: Both have onlookers ask of the couple on the road யார்கொல் அளியர் தாமே; Kuruntokai leaves the question open over the rattling waste, Ainkurunuru answers it with the magandril pair.
links.teaches: The same onlookers' formula could end in fear for the pair (Kuruntokai's dangerous bamboo waste) or in a verdict that they are to be pitied only because they cannot be parted, so அளியர் held both pity and admiration.

links.note: Akananuru 321's foster mother wonders whether the girl will rest with her companion in a small hamlet (சீறூர்) or walk on into the night; Ainkurunuru 382 is told from the hamlet where they rested at nightfall (எல்லிடை அசைந்த ... சீறூர்).
links.teaches: What the foster mother can only imagine is answered from the hamlet itself, where strange women who have daughters feel her pain, so the grief of an elopement was pictured as reaching every house with a girl along the road.

links.note: Natrinai 362's eloping man tells the girl to play gathering velvet mites while he leans on a vengai on guard; Ainkurunuru 383 shows from outside the youth holding the maraam branch while she picks flowers for her doll.
links.teaches: Natrinai gives the man's own promise of guardianship and Ainkurunuru the onlooker's view of his delight in her child's play, so together they fix the eloping hero as an indulgent guardian of a girl still at play rather than a seducer.

links.note: Natrinai 12's girl, leaving, pities the companions who will grieve at her ball and anklets; Ainkurunuru 384's girl, on the road, sends those companions word through brahmins that she went so her beauty might flourish.
links.teaches: The companions are the girl's first thought at both ends of the flight, pitied as she leaves and answered once she is away, and her message turns the pity into a justification that her going completes her mother's care.

links.note: 376's mother curses the fate that joined and sent the girl as without right (அறனில் பால்); 385's girl calls her mother without right (அறனில் யாய்) for keeping her at home.
links.teaches: In two adjoining decades by one poet each side of the elopement denies aram to the other, the mother blaming the fate that joined the lovers and the daughter blaming the mother's guard, so the dispute over whether the going was right is staged from both ends.

links.note: Akananuru 35's girl leaves the sky-touching walled house desolate (வான்தோய் இஞ்சி நன்னகர் புலம்ப); in Ainkurunuru 386 the mother is bewildered in the tall-walled good house (நெடுஞ்சுவர் நல்லில் மருண்ட).
links.teaches: The high wall that in Akananuru stands empty after the girl has slipped it becomes in Ainkurunuru the place where the mother is lost, so the house built to guard a daughter is shown to hold only the one left behind.

links.note: In both a searching woman asks brahmins on the waste road (அந்தணீர், அந்தணிர்) and they answer that they saw the girl (கண்டனம், கண்டனெம்); Kalittokai adds the sandal, pearl and lute argument and says the way never leaves aram.
links.teaches: The scene that Ainkurunuru leaves as a bare eyewitness report of the lover's tenderness was later expanded by Kalittokai into an argument that a daughter belongs to the man she follows, so the brahmins' reply grew from testimony into doctrine.

links.note: Kalittokai's brahmins tell the searching mother not to grieve for the girl who followed the man she chose; Ainkurunuru 388's travellers tell the searcher to rest out the noon heat and go on over the little hill to see the couple's road.
links.teaches: Wayside people meet the pursuer with two different answers, reasons to stop grieving in Kalittokai and directions to go on in Ainkurunuru, so the pursuit was not always treated as something to be talked out of.

links.note: Akananuru 17's foster mother asks whether her girl's small anklet-filled feet (சிலம்புஆர் சீறுடி) can walk the waterless waste; Ainkurunuru 389's searcher asks whether her anklet feet (அம்சிலம் படியே) kept pace with the youth who walked slowly.
links.teaches: The anklet foot is the searching woman's measure in both, but Akananuru weighs it against the road's hardship while Ainkurunuru, told the youth went slowly, weighs it against him, so the same worry could move from the danger of the way to the fitness of the match.

links.note: Natrinai 198 gives the foster mother's own words to those she meets in the waste, describing her daughter and blessing them; Ainkurunuru 390 gives the onlookers' reply to a woman who folds her hands to every good person and asks again and again.
links.teaches: Natrinai lets the searcher speak and Ainkurunuru shows how she looked to those she asked, wandering and worshipping strangers, so the two halves of the wayside exchange make up one recognised scene in which the onlookers' certainty answers her supplication.

source_issues: 387 line 6: மலையிறந்த் தோளே carries a stray pulli (இறந்த்); read மலையிறந்தோளே.
386 line 4: இடும்பை உறவி is hard to construe; read here as a vocative to the mother (உறவி, ant, lost in the walled house); the reading is marked uncertain.
389 line 5: ஒன்றினவோ (did her anklet feet keep pace / were they suited) is read as keeping in step with the slow youth; marked uncertain.
